######## PDF idx 247 ########
SUPERTRAINING
in terms o f factors such as amplitude and direction of movement, and the rate and time of maximal force 
production.
On this basis, as well, isokinetic training and measurement are seen to be so functionally different from 
normal sporting movement as to be relatively useless for giving any information that is accurately applicable to 
the competitive athlete.
Concluding Rem arks
Although technological measurement is invaluable and highly desirable in sport 
and rehabilitation, 
oversimplification of any highly complex situation can lead to serious errors and hinder scientific progress. The 
simplistic central sun and planetary electron model o f the atom was a valuable tool for early 20th century 
physicists, but its replacement by more sophisticated quantum models has advanced our understanding of the 
universe enormously. Unqualified reliance on a single isokinetic model to assess muscular strength and endurance 
is tantamount to permanently accepting the early model of the atom, just because it is easy to work with.
The fact is that human motion involving static and dynamic multiple link components is extremely 
complicated and isokinetic testing can offer only a very simplistic way o f obtaining information on a limited 
number of variables. 
Isokinetic machines are useful for measuring isokinetic actions and changes in two 
dimensions, just as isometric dynamometry is useful for measuring isomctric strength at a given joint angle. 
Extrapolation o f results obtained under these conditions to sporting actions involving other types of muscle 
contraction and patterns of movement is scientifically unacceptable and misleading. Human mobility and stability 
are the integrated result of the appropriate phases of isomctric and non-isokinetic muscle contraction occurring 
with a specific timing in three-dimensional space over specific ranges of joint angle. Multi-faceted human 
movement demands the use of far more versatile and complex technological means, a type of kincsiological 
polygraph which integrates information yielded by concurrent use of devices such as high speed video, EMG, 
myotensiometers, accelerometers and force plates.
The ultimate measure of successful testing and training is unequivocal improvement in the athlete's 
performance, so that sporting movements should still be regarded as the final test of any training or rehabilitation 
regime. In addition, an inexpensive and highly effective alternative to isokinetics is the APRE system based on the 
original work of DeLorme (sec 5.2.2). The convenience of isokinetic testing should be weighed against its high 
cost, limited application and the unsupported claims of manufacturers. The detailed review of the strengths and 
weaknesses of isokinetic methods given by Ostemig (1986) provides further useful information in this regard.
4.2.6.3 S tatic-D ynam ic M ethods
The static-dynamic method of developing muscular strength involves the sequential combination in one exercise of 
isometric and dynamic (auxotonic) muscular activity, each of which can provide its own distinct quantitative 
characteristics. For example, the following variations of static-dynamic exercise have been shown to be effective:
• a 2-3 second isometric contraction (at 80% of one's maximum) is held, followed by explosive concentric 
dynamic work with a load of 30% of maximum
• with both the isometric and dynamic components, a constant load of 75-80% of maximum is used.
In the latter case, for instance, the athlete sinks into the half-squat position with a barbell on his shoulders, holds 
this position for 2 seconds, then with maximal acceleration, jumps upward. After careful landing he repeats the 
exercise.
It has been established experimentally that the first variant of static-dynamic exercise is better than dynamic 
exercise alone for developing speed-strength. The second variant has an equivalent affect on the improvement of 
speed-strength and absolute strength (Dobrovolsky, 1972, 1973).
4.2.6.4 C hoice of M uscle T raining Regim es
One may now ask the question: O f all these regimes, which is the most effective? 
It is difficult to give a 
categorical answer for several reasons:
1. Comprehensive research to evaluate the effectiveness of all the regimes has not been conducted. An attempt, 
for example, to study the effectiveness of eccentric, concentric, isometric and combined regimes revealed
236

######## PDF idx 248 ########
SUPERTRAINING
some advantages of the concentric over the eccentric and isometric method, but the main method using 
combined regimes showed a clear advantage (Plctnev, 1975).
2. Similar comparative research is difficult with respect to controlling the training loads of the different regimes.
3, It is inappropriate to raise the question of the absolute effectiveness of any specific regime. Each of them 
can be the most effective, depending upon factors such as the situation, stage of the annual cycle, level of the 
athlete, the primary regime of muscular work in the special exercise, and the specificity of the strength ability 
acquired as a result of training.
Today it can be ascertained with reasonable certainty that the most rational means of enhancing the effectiveness 
of special strength preparation is to combine the various regimes of muscular work. This has been corroborated 
by several studies (Vorobyev, 1966; Andrianov & Vorobyev, 1969; Kuznetsov, 1970; Verkhoshansky, 1970, 
1972; Slobodyan, 1972; Tatyan, 1974; Pletnev 1975; Khodykin, 1975; Savin, 1974). Such a training combination 
ts selected by taking into consideration its cumulative effect and its correspondence to the specific conditions of 
the sport.
4.2.7 The Use of Training M achines
Recently, training machines for strength development have become very popular in most modem gymnasia. 
However, before machines are used in training, it is important to understand that there are essentially two distinct 
classes of machine:
• Functional resistance machines, whose purpose is to offer resistance in sport specific patterns
• Non-Junctional resistance machines, whose sole purpose is to offer general resistance in non-sport specific 
patterns
An appreciation o f this distinction is vital for many coaches and athletes in the West, because the impressive 
fitness centres in which they often train are usually entirely equipped with non-functional resistance (NFR) 
nuchincs. In fact, the machine training syndrome has become so popular among the average population that it is 
frequently difficult to find adequate free weights or functional resistance (FR) machines in these 'state-of-the-art' 
ccntres. While the use of NFR machines may be adequate for the casual fitness client, it can be profoundly 
counterproductive for sport specific trainees if used in place of FR machines or free weights. Current commer­
cialised emphasis on circuit and cross training has proliferated the use of NFR machines, so the serious athlete 
should become aware of their limitations in sport and rehabilitation, particularly regarding the detrimental effects

than during standing. The increase in stress becomes far greater against resistance, particularly if jerky movements

exciting a force of 50 kg weight (about 490 Newtons) from beginning to end of movement.

standing dumbbell curl, and at least five machines to rival the effectiveness of the flexed-knee deadlift.

physicists, but its replacement by more sophisticated quantum models has advanced our understanding of the 
universe enormously. Unqualified reliance on a single isokinetic model to assess muscular strength and endurance 
is tantamount to permanently accepting the early model of the atom, just because it is easy to work with.
The fact is that human motion involving static and dynamic multiple link components is extremely 
complicated and isokinetic testing can offer only a very simplistic way o f obtaining information on a limited 
number of variables. 
Isokinetic machines are useful for measuring isokinetic actions and changes in two 
dimensions, just as isometric dynamometry is useful for measuring isomctric strength at a given joint angle. 
Extrapolation o f results obtained under these conditions to sporting actions involving other types of muscle 
contraction and patterns of movement is scientifically unacceptable and misleading. Human mobility and stability 
are the integrated result of the appropriate phases of isomctric and non-isokinetic muscle contraction occurring 
with a specific timing in three-dimensional space over specific ranges of joint angle. Multi-faceted human 
movement demands the use of far more versatile and complex technological means, a type of kincsiological 
polygraph which integrates information yielded by concurrent use of devices such as high speed video, EMG, 
myotensiometers, accelerometers and force plates.

performance, so that sporting movements should still be regarded as the final test of any training or rehabilitation

isometric and dynamic (auxotonic) muscular activity, each of which can provide its own distinct quantitative 
characteristics. For example, the following variations of static-dynamic exercise have been shown to be effective:

this position for 2 seconds, then with maximal acceleration, jumps upward. After careful landing he repeats the 
exercise.

######## PDF idx 251 ########
SUPERTRAINING
In other words, more than 24 NFR machines are required to challenge the effectiveness of a circuit 
comprising only four free weights exercises: the clean-and-push press, the squat, deadlift, and biccps curl. In this 
case, the combined cost of these machines is about forty times greater than the combined cost of several sets of 
free weights and the necessary racks. Moreover, the maintenance cost of most NFR machines is considerably 
higher than that of virtually indestructible free weights and the breakdown of machines is a regular occurrence in a 
well-used gymnasium.
4.2.8 The Concept of Sym m etric Training
Asymmetry in leg length, muscle strength, stride length and several other features of human structure and function 
has been blamed as one of the causes of inefficient movement and injury. 
Likewise, imbalances in muscle 
strength between agonists and antagonists, left and right limbs, and in isokinetic muscle endurance, as measured on 
isokinetic devices have been singled out as leading causes of muscle injury (see 4.2.6).
Research, however, has revealed that isokinetically-measurcd discrepancies as large as 10% between 
left/right leg strength and agonist/antagonist strength of the right and left legs do not statistically correlate with a 
major increase in muscular injuries.

compensatory or overflow activity o f muscles other than the ‘prime movers.*

resistance imposed is inadequate to overload the ‘prime movers.* Similarly, the weight trainer who wishes to 
increase hypertrophy or strength of a given muscle selects a weight which forces it to operate at high intensity.

even if certain joints arc restrained as on an isokinetic test machine.

pnme movers. For example, during heavy standing tricep press-downs with cable machines, the abdominal

endurance, but docs not strengthen those muscles which propel the body horizontally.

# Isometric Training Variables and the Adaptations They Bias

**What it is** — Five dials set an isometric stimulus. Natera maps each one to adaptations using a review that the ASR renders as "Orren Schuch." It is almost certainly **Oranchuk, Storey, Nelson & Cronin (2019), *Isometric training and long-term adaptations: effects of muscle length, intensity and intent*** (Scand J Med Sci Sports); two papers in Zotero cite it under that title.
- **Duration.** Short is 2–6 s, moderate about 10 s, long 20–30 s.
- **Muscle length.** Short, moderate or long.
- **Intent.** "Grind" means ramping to maximal force; "explode" means ballistic, reaching force as fast as possible.
- **Intensity.** Low is 30–50% of max; high is 70–100%.
- **Volume.** Reps × sets × duration.

His summary of the review (~22:15–30:14):
- **Muscle mass** is favored by long lengths, higher volume, grind intent and long holds.
- **Fascicle length** changes are equivocal, and length does not change the result. Long lengths favor a **pennation angle** increase.
- **Tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness** respond to high intensity (≥70%), long lengths and **ballistic intent**. Duration matters little, with long "slightly better" for stiffness.
- **Neural adaptation follows intent.** Grind raises EMG at maximal voluntary contraction; explode raises EMG at 0–100 and 100–150 ms.
- **Peak force** does not differ by length. Moderate-to-long lengths spread gains across more of the range, and moderate-to-high intensity gives the best gains.
- **Rate of force development** improves with ballistic intent.
- **Dynamic performance** (squat, CMJ) shows little difference by length or intent.
- **Angle specificity** holds, with some carryover to both shorter and longer lengths.

*(Single-source ASR; verify the slide wording at ~22:15–30:14 and against the paper itself.)*

**Why it works** — Specificity: the tissue and the nervous system adapt to the stimulus they are given. Natera then **selects** from this map for running (~56:03–59:16):
- explode-to-max intent, for tendon and RFD, which also limits hypertrophy;
- **moderate** muscle lengths, avoiding both short lengths and the hypertrophic long end;
- near-max to max intensities (70–100%);
- short holds and low volume, to avoid hypertrophy and fatigue.

He says the method came first and he found the evidence afterward. The link between "moderate length + ballistic" and "better sprint tissue" is his inference, not a tested outcome.

**When to apply** — Use it to reason about *which* dial to turn for a stated goal. Examples: the tendon stiffness bias for an Achilles or patellar tendon RTP late in rehab; RFD for a skill player whose force at 100 ms lags his peak; long, heavier holds in early offseason GPP, when some muscle mass is welcome. **Force-plate hook:** ForceDecks isometric tests separate peak force from force at 50/100/200 ms, so you can check whether an explode block actually moved early force rather than peak force.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's paraphrase of one review, heard through ASR. Read Oranchuk 2019 before citing any single cell of the map. Much of the review's evidence comes from single-joint lab studies in untrained or recreationally trained subjects, so how it generalizes to trained sprinters is unknown. Architecture changes are "questionable," as Natera says himself. Tendon claims (intensity ≥70%, ballistic intent) are **tissue-adaptation claims, untested in this context**. Do not apply the early-rehab analgesic-isometric literature (Rio/Cook) here; that is a different goal 

**Example** — For a DB coming off a patellar tendinopathy flare, pick high intensity (≥70%), ballistic intent, moderate knee angle and short 3 s efforts at low volume. That prescription follows from this map; it is not a validated protocol.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — how the dials are applied in practice.

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate: coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed p. 155, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes. **Inference:** a
further reason, not stated in this section, is that isokinetic symmetry testing measures an
isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent functional, whole-movement asymmetry
accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply** — Direct tension with current Baylor practice: this claim sits in
tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection model
lists symmetry (L/R differences) as an *optional* force-plate reporting category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style) is retained
for targeted return-to-play groups (`method-baseline.md`, citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). The baseline does not itself say symmetry
indices *drive* RTP decisions, only that they are collected as an optional category and
that joint-specific testing continues for RTP groups; this entry should not be read as
claiming the baseline directly contradicts the book on that specific point. **Eric's review
would be needed** to reconcile this 1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based
"correction" with the department's practice: the book's objection is specifically to
*using an isokinetic ratio to drive a correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry
monitoring for tracking purposes more broadly. Modern literature is itself split on how
symmetry data should be used: Afonso et al
([[research-papers/afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]])
and Bishop 2016
([[research-papers/bishop-2016-asymmetries-of-the-lower-limb-the-calculation-conundrum-in-strength-training-and-condition]])
both caution against naive asymmetry-correction approaches, while Callaway 2026
([[research-papers/callaway-2026-group-normative-data-and-arbitrary-asymmetry-thresholds-fail-to-represent-individual-playe]])
argues group-normative asymmetry thresholds fail to
represent individual players, a related but distinct caution about the metric itself
rather than about correcting it.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy,
high-performing athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not
automatically something to "fix": the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a
natural, individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (the preceding
subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); Ch4.2.8 "The Concept of Symmetric
Training" (explicitly deferred by the text itself, not yet ingested, future chapter).

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves
versus curves measured under unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in
the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed
p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15). This "futile" statement sits against the book's own
practice elsewhere: it computes explosive strength (Se) from isometric tension, "0.5 Fmax
over its time" (printed 102, 108); calls starting strength "always produced under
conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

**Why it works** — The authors' own stated reason, given for the force-angle curve
specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the
ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed 90-degree ankle/knee position
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: this entry sits against the book's own
internal contradiction described above (the "futile" statement versus the book's own
isometric-derived explosive-strength, starting-strength, and functional-profile measures),
and against vault evidence of a moderate real relationship. Thomas et al 2015
([[research-papers/thomas-2015-an-investigation-into-the-relationship-between-maximum-isometric-strength-and-vertical-jum]]) found isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP) impulse correlates
with countermovement-jump and squat-jump peak force and power (r = 0.49-0.64), though not
with jump height. **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has no
value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance."
The caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests, alone, to infer
dynamic, functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all; the entry's
`contested` rating reflects that the book itself does not consistently follow its own
caution.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak measured at the wrong joint angle for the sport
skill can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive performance. The device itself cannot
measure rate of force development or explosive strength directly, per the authors' own
"futile" statement above, so a slow-RFD finding from an isometric test should not be cited
as evidence of that device's own output. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],

# Isometric Training Variables and the Adaptations They Bias

**What it is** — Five dials set an isometric stimulus. Natera maps each one to adaptations using a review that the ASR renders as "Orren Schuch." It is almost certainly **Oranchuk, Storey, Nelson & Cronin (2019), *Isometric training and long-term adaptations: effects of muscle length, intensity and intent*** (Scand J Med Sci Sports); two papers in Zotero cite it under that title.
- **Duration.** Short is 2–6 s, moderate about 10 s, long 20–30 s.
- **Muscle length.** Short, moderate or long.
- **Intent.** "Grind" means ramping to maximal force; "explode" means ballistic, reaching force as fast as possible.
- **Intensity.** Low is 30–50% of max; high is 70–100%.
- **Volume.** Reps × sets × duration.

His summary of the review (~22:15–30:14):
- **Muscle mass** is favored by long lengths, higher volume, grind intent and long holds.
- **Fascicle length** changes are equivocal, and length does not change the result. Long lengths favor a **pennation angle** increase.
- **Tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness** respond to high intensity (≥70%), long lengths and **ballistic intent**. Duration matters little, with long "slightly better" for stiffness.
- **Neural adaptation follows intent.** Grind raises EMG at maximal voluntary contraction; explode raises EMG at 0–100 and 100–150 ms.
- **Peak force** does not differ by length. Moderate-to-long lengths spread gains across more of the range, and moderate-to-high intensity gives the best gains.
- **Rate of force development** improves with ballistic intent.
- **Dynamic performance** (squat, CMJ) shows little difference by length or intent.
- **Angle specificity** holds, with some carryover to both shorter and longer lengths.

*(Single-source ASR; verify the slide wording at ~22:15–30:14 and against the paper itself.)*

**Why it works** — Specificity: the tissue and the nervous system adapt to the stimulus they are given. Natera then **selects** from this map for running (~56:03–59:16):
- explode-to-max intent, for tendon and RFD, which also limits hypertrophy;
- **moderate** muscle lengths, avoiding both short lengths and the hypertrophic long end;
- near-max to max intensities (70–100%);
- short holds and low volume, to avoid hypertrophy and fatigue.

He says the method came first and he found the evidence afterward. The link between "moderate length + ballistic" and "better sprint tissue" is his inference, not a tested outcome.

**When to apply** — Use it to reason about *which* dial to turn for a stated goal. Examples: the tendon stiffness bias for an Achilles or patellar tendon RTP late in rehab; RFD for a skill player whose force at 100 ms lags his peak; long, heavier holds in early offseason GPP, when some muscle mass is welcome. **Force-plate hook:** ForceDecks isometric tests separate peak force from force at 50/100/200 ms, so you can check whether an explode block actually moved early force rather than peak force.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's paraphrase of one review, heard through ASR. Read Oranchuk 2019 before citing any single cell of the map. Much of the review's evidence comes from single-joint lab studies in untrained or recreationally trained subjects, so how it generalizes to trained sprinters is unknown. Architecture changes are "questionable," as Natera says himself. Tendon claims (intensity ≥70%, ballistic intent) are **tissue-adaptation claims, untested in this context**. Do not apply the early-rehab analgesic-isometric literature (Rio/Cook) here; that is a different goal 

**Example** — For a DB coming off a patellar tendinopathy flare, pick high intensity (≥70%), ballistic intent, moderate knee angle and short 3 s efforts at low volume. That prescription follows from this map; it is not a validated protocol.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — how the dials are applied in practice.

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate: coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed p. 155, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes. **Inference:** a
further reason, not stated in this section, is that isokinetic symmetry testing measures an
isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent functional, whole-movement asymmetry
accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply** — Direct tension with current Baylor practice: this claim sits in
tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection model
lists symmetry (L/R differences) as an *optional* force-plate reporting category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style) is retained
for targeted return-to-play groups (`method-baseline.md`, citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). The baseline does not itself say symmetry
indices *drive* RTP decisions, only that they are collected as an optional category and
that joint-specific testing continues for RTP groups; this entry should not be read as
claiming the baseline directly contradicts the book on that specific point. **Eric's review
would be needed** to reconcile this 1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based
"correction" with the department's practice: the book's objection is specifically to
*using an isokinetic ratio to drive a correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry
monitoring for tracking purposes more broadly. Modern literature is itself split on how
symmetry data should be used: Afonso et al
([[research-papers/afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]])
and Bishop 2016
([[research-papers/bishop-2016-asymmetries-of-the-lower-limb-the-calculation-conundrum-in-strength-training-and-condition]])
both caution against naive asymmetry-correction approaches, while Callaway 2026
([[research-papers/callaway-2026-group-normative-data-and-arbitrary-asymmetry-thresholds-fail-to-represent-individual-playe]])
argues group-normative asymmetry thresholds fail to
represent individual players, a related but distinct caution about the metric itself
rather than about correcting it.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy,
high-performing athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not
automatically something to "fix": the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a
natural, individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (the preceding
subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); Ch4.2.8 "The Concept of Symmetric
Training" (explicitly deferred by the text itself, not yet ingested, future chapter).

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves
versus curves measured under unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in
the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed
p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15). This "futile" statement sits against the book's own
practice elsewhere: it computes explosive strength (Se) from isometric tension, "0.5 Fmax
over its time" (printed 102, 108); calls starting strength "always produced under
conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

**Why it works** — The authors' own stated reason, given for the force-angle curve
specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the
ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed 90-degree ankle/knee position
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: this entry sits against the book's own
internal contradiction described above (the "futile" statement versus the book's own
isometric-derived explosive-strength, starting-strength, and functional-profile measures),
and against vault evidence of a moderate real relationship. Thomas et al 2015
([[research-papers/thomas-2015-an-investigation-into-the-relationship-between-maximum-isometric-strength-and-vertical-jum]]) found isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP) impulse correlates
with countermovement-jump and squat-jump peak force and power (r = 0.49-0.64), though not
with jump height. **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has no
value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance."
The caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests, alone, to infer
dynamic, functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all; the entry's
`contested` rating reflects that the book itself does not consistently follow its own
caution.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak measured at the wrong joint angle for the sport
skill can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive performance. The device itself cannot
measure rate of force development or explosive strength directly, per the authors' own
"futile" statement above, so a slow-RFD finding from an isometric test should not be cited
as evidence of that device's own output. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# Handford et al. 2024 — A taxonomy of eccentric training methods

> **Citation**
> Handford, M. J., Bright, T. E., Mundy, P., Lake, J., Theis, N., & Hughes, J. D. (2024). A conceptual framework of different eccentric training methods. *Strength and Conditioning Journal, 46*(2), 148–158. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000781

## Why it was promoted

This paper supplies a clearer vocabulary for programming and discussing eccentric training without conflating a muscle action, an exercise phase, a coaching cue, and an intended adaptation.

## Research question

How can eccentric motions and eccentric-training methods be classified so that researchers and practitioners describe the intended mechanical task and adaptation more precisely?

## Population and context

- Participants: None; this is a conceptual narrative review.
- Sport and level: General strength-and-conditioning application.
- Training or return-to-play context: Exercise classification and program design.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: The paper proposes terminology and a working framework; it is not a comparative intervention or systematic review.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Conceptual narrative synthesis.
- Exposure or intervention: None.
- Comparator: Five proposed eccentric-motion categories and the training methods mapped to them.
- Measurements and outcomes: No pooled or newly collected outcome data.
- Analysis: Conceptual differentiation based on prior literature and applied examples.

## Key findings

- The framework distinguishes maximal, overcoming, rebound, dissipating, and deceleration eccentric motions according to whether the load can be stopped or reversed, the intended braking strategy, and stretch-shortening-cycle behavior. [p. 3]
- The authors map methods such as tempo work, plyometrics, accentuated eccentric loading, and accelerated eccentric loading to different motions and intended responses. [p. 6]
- The framework is explicitly not evidence that one eccentric method is superior; its purpose is terminology and selection clarity. [p. 9]

## Limitations and applicability

- The paper identifies limitations in earlier models but does not report a systematic search, evidence grading, or comparative intervention. [p. 3]
- Several links between methods and adaptations in the framework are theoretical rather than empirically established, which the figure distinguishes. [p. 6]
- Practitioner transfer limitation: Category assignment helps specify a program but does not establish an effective dose for a particular athlete or rehabilitation stage.

## Practitioner interpretation

====
36:- Applies broadly to performance testing but does not validate injury or performance thresholds.

# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, shorter intervals
between sessions) does not reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed
some way. (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
===
# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975), the
authors state that the joint angle at which maximum muscular tension is exerted during
training determines how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF p. 113, printed p. 102.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no cellular mechanism in this passage; they treat it as
an established empirical regularity. The text does not state the training mode used in the
cited studies. **Inference:** the cited studies were likely isometric single-angle
training, since that is the standard method for producing tension at one fixed joint angle
(not confirmed in the text; verify against the original studies). A further plausible
mechanism (also not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when deciding where in the range to bias a
strength exercise for an athlete who needs broad strength across a joint's full range (most

# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts

**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, shorter intervals
between sessions) does not reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed
some way. (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
===
# Training at a Joint's Longest-Muscle-Length Angle Transfers More Evenly; Training at a Shortened Angle Gains More but Transfers Less

**What it is** — Citing Zatsiorsky & Raitsin (1974) and Raitsin & Sarsania (1975), the
authors state that the joint angle at which maximum muscular tension is exerted during
training determines how that strength gain transfers to other joint angles. If maximum
muscular force is trained at the angle corresponding to the muscle's greatest length (the
smallest degree of flexion for active flexion work, or the least extension for extension
work), the resulting strength increase transfers relatively uniformly to other joint
angles. If maximum force is instead trained with the joint significantly flexed and the
muscle in a shortened state, the resulting strength increase at that specific angle is
larger, but transfers comparatively poorly to other joint angles, with transfer falling off
further the farther the target angle is from the trained one. (PDF p. 113, printed p. 102.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no cellular mechanism in this passage; they treat it as
an established empirical regularity. The text does not state the training mode used in the
cited studies. **Inference:** the cited studies were likely isometric single-angle
training, since that is the standard method for producing tension at one fixed joint angle
(not confirmed in the text; verify against the original studies). A further plausible
mechanism (also not stated in this passage) is that training at a lengthened position
recruits a joint-angle range closer to what most functional tasks pass through on the way to
lockout, so gains generalize across the arc, whereas training in a fully shortened position
trains a narrow, less commonly used part of the strength curve, producing a large but
narrowly-tuned adaptation (consistent with the general specificity principle in

# Round-1 review: Supertraining 4.2.4-4.2.9 (Ch4-2b), 20 entries

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, round 1). Date: 2026-09-27.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. Page key: PDF idx (0-based) = printed + 11. Text read directly from PDF idx 234-253 (printed 223-242) with PyMuPDF. Page images opened for Figs 4.11 and 4.12 (PDF 236, p.225), 4.13 and 4.14 (PDF 238, p.227), 4.16 (PDF 245, p.234). Fig 4.8 sits at PDF 233 (p.222, 4.2.3 kinetic-energy stimulation). No entry in scope cites it, so it is out of scope and I did not review it.
Vault and staging cross-checked: Moyer `framework--isometric-training-variables-and-adaptations`, Handford 2024, Bishop 2016, Supertraining Ch2 `heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength`, Ch2 `claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer`, Ch3 `claim--natural-asymmetry-caution-against-isokinetic-symmetry-correction`, Ch1 `framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology`, Ch1 `claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus`, `docs/method-baseline.md`. All 32 wikilink targets in the 20 entries resolve (staging or vault).

## Headline checks

- **`proven`: 0 of 20.** Checked. Nothing to lower.
- **`contested`: 2 of 20, not 3.** The brief expected three. Only `claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings` and `heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity` carry it. Under the brief's rule (X on one page, not-X on another: record both, set `contested`), I recommend **raising `heuristic--choice-of-muscle-training-regime-favor-combination` to `contested`**: p.231 says "premature" and p.237 says "reasonable certainty". I also recommend **considering it for `heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity`**: p.233 gives Vorobyev's sport-specific targets and, on the same page, calls any optimal ratio "meaningless". Details in the rows.
- **Isokinetic "physics limitation" entry:** attributed to the authors ("The authors call ... a 'faulty basic assumption'"). It is the book's argument, not the writer's. But the entry merges two separate limitations the book keeps apart (see its row).
- **Machine-marketing entry:** the judgments are attributed to the authors in the body. One "implied mechanism" is unlabelled.
- **Symmetry entry:** the body is faithful, but the title and "Why it works" go beyond the book.
- **Voice:** "the authors" is used throughout. The one Verkhoshansky-specific sentence ("Verkhoshansky stresses", p.229) is rendered correctly. No voice errors found.

**Patterns, for the fixer.** This writer labelled inferences much better than earlier waves: most Examples are either the book's own or begin "Inference:". The failures fall into five groups:
- (a) **Locators off by one page or more** in 8 entries, listed per row.
- (b) **Unrecorded internal contradictions:** the 6 s vs 8 s vs 10 s hold (p.226), eccentric p.230 vs p.231, regime choice p.231 vs p.237, the ratio page p.233, Thistle 1967 p.232 vs p.235, and duration vs intensity threshold (p.224 vs p.22-23).
- (c) **Unlabelled mechanisms and judgments** in 7 entries.
- (d) **One reversed sentence** (FR/NFR).
- (e) **One false "Eric's baseline:" claim** (NFR entry).

## Headline checks

- **`proven`: 0 of 20.** Checked. Nothing to lower.
- **`contested`: 2 of 20, not 3.** The brief expected three. Only `claim--eccentric-vs-concentric-training-adaptation-contradictory-findings` and `heuristic--isokinetic-testing-limitations-for-functional-sport-specificity` carry it. Under the brief's rule (X on one page, not-X on another: record both, set `contested`), I recommend **raising `heuristic--choice-of-muscle-training-regime-favor-combination` to `contested`**: p.231 says "premature" and p.237 says "reasonable certainty". I also recommend **considering it for `heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity`**: p.233 gives Vorobyev's sport-specific targets and, on the same page, calls any optimal ratio "meaningless". Details in the rows.
- **Isokinetic "physics limitation" entry:** attributed to the authors ("The authors call ... a 'faulty basic assumption'"). It is the book's argument, not the writer's. But the entry merges two separate limitations the book keeps apart (see its row).
- **Machine-marketing entry:** the judgments are attributed to the authors in the body. One "implied mechanism" is unlabelled.
- **Symmetry entry:** the body is faithful, but the title and "Why it works" go beyond the book.
- **Voice:** "the authors" is used throughout. The one Verkhoshansky-specific sentence ("Verkhoshansky stresses", p.229) is rendered correctly. No voice errors found.

**Patterns, for the fixer.** This writer labelled inferences much better than earlier waves: most Examples are either the book's own or begin "Inference:". The failures fall into five groups:
- (a) **Locators off by one page or more** in 8 entries, listed per row.
- (b) **Unrecorded internal contradictions:** the 6 s vs 8 s vs 10 s hold (p.226), eccentric p.230 vs p.231, regime choice p.231 vs p.237, the ratio page p.233, Thistle 1967 p.232 vs p.235, and duration vs intensity threshold (p.224 vs p.22-23).
- (c) **Unlabelled mechanisms and judgments** in 7 entries.
- (d) **One reversed sentence** (FR/NFR).
- (e) **One false "Eric's baseline:" claim** (NFR entry).

## Entry table

| claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate.md | FIX | (1) Locator: entry says "(PDF pp. 235, printed pp. 223-224". The Hettinger-Muller sentence starts on PDF 234 / p.223 ("Hettinger and Muller (1953, 1955) established ... increase strength about 5% per") and ends on PDF 235 / p.224. (2) When NOT says "1950s studies, corroborated only by a 1970 review". The source says the reverse: the research "produced rather contradictory data (see review by Verkhoshansky, 1970)" (p.224). The 1970 review is not corroboration. input.message:
I reviewed all 20 entries against the book pages. Result: **1 GO, 19 FIX, 0 NO-GO. Overall verdict: GO AFTER FIXES.** The report is written in the prompt's format. That is the only file I wrote. I read each page's text from the PDF (PDF 234-253, printed 223-242) and opened Figs 4.11, 4.12, 4.13, 4.14 and 4.16 as page images. Fig 4.8 is on PDF 233 (section 4.2.3), and no entry in scope cites it.

- **GO:** only `claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular`.
- **Hettinger-Muller:** the gain rate and protocol are correct: two-thirds of max, 6 s, daily, 10 weeks, about 5% a week, printed pp. 223-224.
- **`proven`:** none of the 20 use it.
- **`contested`:** only 2 entries carry it, not 3. The eccentric-vs-concentric entry records only one side. The book calls the findings "often contradictory" on p.230, then on p.231 says eccentric training "tends to produce greater and more rapid increases" (Hortobagyi 2000). That p.231 statement needs to go in with its page, plus a stated reason. The isokinetic-testing entry states its reason but gives no pages. I recommend raising the regime-choice entry to `contested`: p.231 calls any definitive answer "premature", p.237 claims "reasonable certainty". The quad:hamstring ratio entry may deserve it too: p.233 gives sport-specific target ratios, then calls any optimal ratio "meaningless".
- **Isokinetic "physics limitation":** the argument is correctly credited to the authors. But the entry merges two limits the book keeps apart. One is that most injuries occur in the acceleration phases, which the authors assert with no citation. The other is the missing elastic energy of natural movement.
- **Machine-marketing entry:** the judgments are credited to the authors. One "implied mechanism" is unlabelled, and there is no caveat that the book's Newton's-law rebuttal does not address how resistance varies with joint angle.
- **Symmetry entry:** the title's "Usefully Asymmetric" goes beyond the book. In Yushkevich's data asymmetry peaked at Class 2 and fell as mastery rose.
- **Voice:** "the authors" is used correctly throughout.

Two errors need fixing before promotion:
1. **Reversed sentence** in `framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines`. The book (p.238) says the facility with only non-functional (fixed-pattern) machines gives the inferior conditioning; the entry says the pulley facility does. I rated it FIX rather than NO-GO because it is a subordinate clause with a one-line correction.
2. **False "Eric's baseline:" claim** in `heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use`. It says the department avoids seated machine testing, but `method-baseline.md` line 60 says the department runs a seated isometric calf raise on ForceDecks.

The other fixes fall into four groups:
- **Wrong page references in 8 entries.** The isokinetic-method entry is off by one full page; it should be PDF 242-243 / printed 231-232.
- **Contradictions inside the book that entries leave out:**
  - three hold lengths on one page: 6 s, 8 s and 10 s (p.226);
  - the two eccentric pages;
  - the regime-choice pages;
  - the ratio page;
  - the Thistle 1967 study, cited as support on p.232 and called unproven on p.235;
  - duration-over-intensity (p.224) against the book's own intensity threshold (p.22-23).
- **Unlabelled mechanisms or judgments in 7 entries:** priming, loadless, symmetry, marketing, static-dynamic, isolation, execution protocol.
- **Figure misreadings:**
  - Fig 4.12's curves are labelled "Explosive", not reflexive.
  - Fig 4.16's caption puts full extension at 90°, so "at 80 degrees" means nearly straight. The figure has no source, but the entry credits it to Vorobyev and Stephens & Reid.

I found no true duplicates in the vault. The report also lists 5 missing ideas and 4 reciprocal-link suggestions.

One citation needs checking before anyone relies on it. I cited Wilke et al 1999 (*Spine*) as modern evidence against the book's "sitting always loads the discs more" claim. It is not in the vault, so I marked it "verify".
